description: Why Single-Line Queuing Outperforms Multi-Line Queuing: A Markovian Perspective
summary:
Introduction Whenever you step into a bank or a grocery store, you encounter one of two queueing designs:
Multi-Line Queuing ($c \times M/M/1$): Each register or counter has its own dedicated line. Customers pick a line and wait. Single-Line Queuing ($M/M/c$): A single “serpentine” line feeds into all available counters. The person at the front goes to the next open station. While multi-line setups might feel faster because individual lines look shorter, single-line systems are mathematically superior in both average wait time and queue stability. Using Markov Chain theory and Queueing Theory, we can prove why pooling capacity eliminates systemic inefficiencies.
title: Single vs Multi Lane Waiting

Why Run Local AI? No Root / Sudo Required: Runs completely within user space under your home directory. 100% Private & Air-Gapped: Zero external telemetry, no data scraping by third parties, and all inference remains strictly on localhost. Cost Effective: No API subscriptions, token charges, or usage caps. Web Search Extensibility: Open-WebUI can optionally connect to search backends (such as DuckDuckGo / SearXNG) for live Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). Scope: This guide focuses on a secure, localhost-only developer setup on Linux (Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, Fedora). Native installers are also available for Windows and macOS. 1. description: How to resolve false-positive missing import errors in VS Code and VSCodium when using Conda environments.
summary:
If you are working with Conda environments, you might notice that VSCodium or VS Code shows “import not found” errors (red squiggly lines) even though your code runs perfectly fine in the terminal.
This happens because the IDE’s Python extension doesn’t automatically know which Conda environment to use for its background linting and IntelliSense. By explicitly setting the interpreter path, you tell the IDE exactly where to look for your installed packages.

description: A practical, modern guide to package and environment management with Conda and Miniforge.
summary:
Why Conda? Conda is an open-source package management and environment management system designed for scientific computing, machine learning, and multi-language development (Python, R, C/C++, etc.).
Key advantages of Conda include:
Isolated Environments: Every project maintains its own isolated dependency sandbox, preventing version conflicts between libraries (e.g. PyTorch 2.x vs TensorFlow 2.x). Binary Non-Python Dependencies: Unlike pip, which primarily manages Python wheels and packages, Conda can install compiled system libraries (such as CUDA runtimes, cuDNN, OpenBLAS, Graphviz, and HDF5) directly into your environment without requiring root/sudo privileges. Cross-Platform Consistency: Ensures identical dependency resolution across Linux, macOS, and Windows. Installation: Miniforge vs. Anaconda While full Anaconda includes a large bundle of pre-installed GUI tools and packages, the recommended modern standard is Miniforge. Miniforge is a minimalist, community-driven installer pre-configured with conda-forge as the default channel (avoiding commercial licensing restrictions of Anaconda’s default channel).
title: Conda Essentials: Complete Guide & Cheat Sheet

summary: Overview Why and when do we need linear regression? In a nutshell, linear regression is used to predict data that has a linear relationship. That means all the datapoints are roughly on a straight line (in 2D), resp. on a hyperplane (in 3D). Firstly, we find some expression for the linear relationship (e.g. in 2D: $y=a\cdot x + b$; where $a$ is the slope and $b$ is the y-intercept). Secondly, we use this expression to insert some data where we only know the $x$ value, but want to predict their unknown $y$ value.
title: Linear Regression

summary:
Introduction In our previous article, Backpropagation in Standard Calculus, we derived the gradient update equations using scalar notation. While standard calculus builds an intuitive understanding of how error flows through individual connections, writing code using scalar loops is computationally inefficient.
In practice, modern machine learning libraries (like PyTorch or TensorFlow) compute updates over entire layers simultaneously using Matrix Calculus and linear algebra routines optimized for GPUs.
This article formalizes backpropagation in vector and matrix notation.
title: Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus

summary:
Introduction This article gives a quick overview over the feedforward phase of a Neural Network.
Nodes A Neural Network is made of many Nodes that are connected to each other. Each Node itself is a very basic unit that does only do three things.
Multiply each input with a weight and sum all inputs up. $y_{in} = \sum_{i=0}^m w_i\cdot x_i$, where $m$ is the number of inputs. Process the single, scalar input value by some activation function $y_{out}=f(y_{in})$ where $y_{in}$ is the result from step 1 and $y_{out}$ is the result from step 1 after being applied to the activation function. Output the result $y_{out}$ to the next node So, a single node pretty much looks like this:
title: Feedforward Phase

summary:
Introduction This article explains backpropagation of a Neural Network using standard scalar calculus notation. If you want to know how backpropagation is done using vectors and matrices, read this article: Backpropagation in Matrix Calculus
Learning Process Consider a 2-layer Neural Network (one hidden layer and one output layer) as shown below. We want to train the network so that the training inputs $x$ correctly produce the expected target labels $t$.
For training, we use a dataset containing paired samples $(x, t)$. Each pair is used to adjust the network parameters to minimize the difference between the network’s prediction $y$ and the actual target $t$. Thinking of the network as a function $y = f(x)$, our goal is to adjust $f(x)$ until the prediction error is as small as possible. A smaller error means the predictions closely match ground truth labels.
title: Backpropagation in Standard Calculus
